# Findings

*Generated by `python -m analysis.findings`. Every figure below is computed from the warehouse at build time.*

## Scope

| | |
|---|---|
| Flights | 33,653,101 |
| Window | 2021-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (17 carriers, 381 airports, 7,090 airframes) |
| On-time arrival (A14) | 77.97% |
| Completion factor | 98.05% |
| Cancellation rate | 1.70% |
| Mean arrival delay | 6.6 min |
| 90th percentile arrival delay | 41 min |

## Finding 1 — 38.8% of all delay is inherited, not caused

Of 470.7M delay minutes, 288.2M originated with the flight
that reported them and 182.5M arrived on a late aircraft from an earlier
leg. At $98.41/block minute the inherited share alone is
**$17.96B** of direct operating cost over five years.

Inherited delay has no cause of its own. Every minute of it was created
somewhere else and moved here by an airframe, which means it cannot be fixed
at the flight that reports it -- only at the flight that started it.

## Finding 2 — the propagation mechanism is slack, and the model checks out

Delay passes through a turn only to the extent the ground time cannot absorb
it: `predicted = max(0, inbound_delay - slack)`, where slack is the scheduled
turn minus the fastest turn that operator has actually achieved at that
station.

Across 5,375,141 turns receiving an aircraft more than 15 minutes late, the model
predicts a mean of 23.3 minutes passed on. The airlines themselves
reported 21.2. Correlation between the two, computed independently:
**0.784**.

The dose-response is monotonic. Among turns receiving an aircraft 30-60
minutes late, those with under 15 minutes of slack passed on
27.3 minutes and departed late 96% of the
time; those with 90+ minutes passed on 1.1 minutes and
departed late 15% of the time.

## Finding 3 — the same delay costs 13x more in the morning

A root delay departing at 08:00 goes on to delay
0.75 further flights and 39.4 further minutes. The same
delay at 21:00 costs 0.06 legs and
4.9 minutes -- the aircraft is done for the day and there is
nothing left downstream to break.

Amplification peaks at 2.44x around
11:00: for every minute the root
flight lost, the network lost 2.44.

## Finding 4 — so buffer the morning? No. The data says the opposite

The obvious response to Finding 3 is to protect the morning bank with extra
ground time. Simulating +10 minutes of slack on every turn and re-running the
propagation model says that would be close to worthless.

Buffer efficiency -- delay minutes avoided per buffer minute spent -- averages
**0.014** across turns before 09:00, against a peak of
**0.185** at 19:00. The reason is simple once
seen: aircraft turning in the early morning slept at the station overnight.
They arrive on time because nothing has happened yet. There is no delay there
to absorb, so slack has nothing to do.

Buffer works where late aircraft actually are, which is the afternoon. But by
then amplification has fallen to
1.34x and much of the day's
damage is already done. **No hour of the day reaches an efficiency of 1.0.**
Blanket schedule padding does not pay for itself in delay minutes at any hour,
which is a finding, not a failure -- it rules out the intuitive answer.

## Finding 5 — the lever that does work is prevention before noon

If slack cannot help the morning, the only remaining lever is stopping the
root delay from happening. 55.5M minutes of *carrier-controllable*
root delay -- crew, maintenance, boarding, fuelling, baggage -- originated
between 05:00 and 11:00 over the five years, and it carried an average
amplification of 2.10x.

Preventing 20% of it removes **23.3M network delay minutes**, worth
roughly **$459M a year** in direct operating cost. That is the
recommendation this analysis supports, and it is aimed at station operations
before noon -- not at the schedule.



## Finding 6 — the carrier table, and what sits underneath it

| Carrier | Type | Flights | A14 | Inherited share |

| Republic Airways | Regional | 1,592,363 | 80.88% | 34.5% |
| SkyWest Airlines | Regional | 3,746,635 | 80.75% | 21.7% |
| Envoy Air | Regional | 1,310,534 | 79.57% | 41.2% |
| United Airlines | Network | 3,361,244 | 78.70% | 39.3% |
| Alaska Airlines | Network | 1,154,090 | 77.83% | 37.3% |
| PSA Airlines | Regional | 1,107,911 | 77.73% | 47.9% |
| Mesa Airlines | Regional | 274,588 | 77.26% | 35.7% |
| Southwest Airlines | Low-cost | 6,621,558 | 76.60% | 50.4% |
| American Airlines | Network | 4,509,034 | 75.04% | 45.2% |
| Spirit Airlines | Ultra low-cost | 1,143,250 | 73.87% | 28.4% |
| Allegiant Air | Ultra low-cost | 596,406 | 71.33% | 40.7% |
| Frontier Airlines | Ultra low-cost | 876,855 | 69.77% | 48.6% |
| JetBlue Airways | Low-cost | 1,222,307 | 69.57% | 38.0% |
The inherited-share column explains the ranking better than the A14 column
describes it. Delta carries 28.4%
inherited delay and schedules a median 40 minutes of
slack at ATL, with 16% of turns tight.
Southwest carries 50.4%
and schedules 13 minutes at DEN, with
59% tight.

That is not a quality gap, it is a business model. High utilisation is how the
low-cost fare exists; the cascade is what it costs. The two numbers belong in
the same sentence.

One caveat the table cannot escape: BTS reports the OPERATING carrier. Endeavor
and Horizon top this ranking as regional operators flying short stages under
Delta and Alaska brands, and their passengers booked Delta and Alaska.



## Finding 7 — December 2022, with a control group

A winter storm hit the US network on 21-23 December 2022. Every carrier flew
into the same weather, which makes the days that follow a natural experiment:
the storm is the treatment, the other carriers are the control, and the only
thing that differs is how each airline's rotations absorbed it.


| Date | Southwest cancelled | All other carriers |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2022-12-20 | 0.3% | 2.2% |
| 2022-12-21 | 4.5% | 2.4% |
| 2022-12-22 | 26.2% | 9.6% |
| 2022-12-23 | 36.9% | 25.2% |
| 2022-12-24 | 43.7% | 15.7% |
| 2022-12-25 | 51.6% | 11.4% |
| 2022-12-26 | 77.5% | 6.7% |
| 2022-12-27 | 69.7% | 2.9% |
| 2022-12-28 | 64.4% | 2.4% |
| 2022-12-29 | 61.2% | 0.8% |
| 2022-12-30 | 1.1% | 0.6% |
| 2022-12-31 | 1.0% | 1.4% |
Both groups break together on the 22nd. From the 26th the control group is
essentially recovered at 6.7%
while Southwest peaks at **77.5%** on the same day and stays above
60% for three more.

The weather stopped and the cancellations did not. What continued was the
cascade: aircraft and crews out of position, every recovery attempt inheriting
from the last. This is Finding 1 at full scale -- a network whose delay was
almost entirely inherited by then, with no root cause left to fix.
